pr_title: Apply [[nodiscard]] to functions returning error codes
pr_body:
<!-- Enter a brief description/summary of your PR here. What does it fix/what does it change/how was it tested (even manually, if necessary)? -->
## Summary of the Pull Request
Functions returning status codes should use [[nodiscard]] as [mentioned recently](https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/pull/897#discussion_r286205725) by @adiviness.

They should also use noexcept, but that's a much more invasive change, so this issue is just about [[nodiscard]].

<!-- Other than the issue solved, is this relevant to any other issues/existing PRs? --> 
## References
#897 

<!-- Please review the items on the PR checklist before submitting-->
## PR Checklist
* [X] Closes #951
* [X] CLA signed. If not, go over [here](https://cla.opensource.microsoft.com/microsoft/Terminal) and sign the CLA
* [X] Tests added/passed
* [ ] Requires documentation to be updated
* [ ] I've discussed this with core contributors already. If not checked, I'm ready to accept this work might be rejected in favor of a different grand plan. Issue number where discussion took place: #897 

<!-- Provide a more detailed description of the PR, other things fixed or any additional comments/features here -->
## Detailed Description of the Pull Request / Additional comments
- applied [[nodiscard]] for all HRESULT, LRESULT, and NTSTATUS functions
- fixed IntelliSense declaration complaints leading to function not
  implemented warnings
- deleted declared but never implemented functions
- fixed unused parameter warnings

Please note I only checked for functions that had a declaration in a header file of some kind, so there might still be some functions only defined and used within .cpp files that don't have [[nodiscard]] applied.

How verified:
- bcz dbg
- opencon
- testcon
- VS2019 debug build

Functions returning status codes should use [[nodiscard]] as [mentioned recently](https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/pull/897#discussion_r286205725) by @adiviness.

They should also use noexcept, but that's a much more invasive change, so this issue is just about [[nodiscard]].

IntelliSense inconsistent definition warning `()` vs. `(VOID)`.
I'm shocked the compiler even allowed this.
I don't want to start a holy war here, but `i++` vs `++i`?
There was a point in time or situation where `++i` was faster than `i++`. Not sure if it still holds.

My intent has nothing to do with speed; it's a personal habit of mine to avoid postfix wherever possible because it's too easy to write an off-by-one bug.  Before anyone asks, the ISO C++ guidelines are completely silent on this as far as I can tell; the only cursory reference I can find is to user-defined operators:

> Flag an unused return value from a user-defined non-defaulted postfix operator++ or operator-- function. Prefer using the prefix form instead.

Yes, historically, pre-increment/decrement was "faster" than post, because post creates a copy of the original value before incrementing, whereas pre doesn't.  However, in this case, I can see no actual difference in generated code so I imagine the compiler optimizes it away:

https://godbolt.org/z/1_dVhl

To put differently, I guess my reasoning would be that postfix form should be used only when the code explicitly wants the sequenced post-increment behavior.  Otherwise, code should always use prefix form.

The real problem with postfix form is that the author/reader suddenly has to be acutely aware of sequencing points and [undefined behavior](https://herbsutter.com/2014/12/01/a-quick-poll-about-order-of-evaluation/
).  There's a great thread on stackoverflow the lists [many examples](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/949433/why-are-these-constructs-using-pre-and-post-increment-undefined-behavior).

However, this is definitely a question of project and personal style, and is not a correctness issue or a guidelines issues.  So, I'm happy to adopt whatever the project deems as the preferred style.

I am totally good with adopting `++i` as the preferred behavior given the advantages you list. 

It's just been my forever habit (since I learned to code) to do postfix. I could be retrained for a convincing benefit. And we could enforce it to some degree. Depends what the other folks think (@zadjii-msft, @adiviness, @DHowett-MSFT).
I'm a fan of prefix by default, postfix where necessary, basically for the reasons listed above.
